title: John's Question and Jesus' Invitation
summary: From prison, John the Baptist sends to ask whether Jesus is the one who was to come, and Jesus answers with the works the prophets foretold. Jesus then praises John as more than a prophet, rebukes a generation that rejected both John and himself, and pronounces woes on the Galilean towns that saw his miracles and did not repent. The chapter ends with Jesus thanking the Father for revealing these things to little children and inviting the weary to come to him for rest.
story: The twelve have been sent out, and Matthew now turns to how Jesus himself is being received. The answer is mixed and growing darker. John, who announced Jesus in chapter 3, is in prison and uncertain. The crowds treat both John and Jesus like children who will not join any game. The towns around the lake, where most of Jesus' miracles were done, have not changed. Chapter 11 opens a new section of the Gospel (running through chapter 12) in which rejection becomes the main theme, and yet it closes with one of the tenderest invitations in Scripture. The pairing is deliberate: hidden from the proud, the kingdom is opened to the tired and the humble.
historical:
Matthew 14 will tell how Herod Antipas arrested John for condemning his marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing near the end of the first century, also describes John's arrest and execution by Antipas, and says it took place at Machaerus, a Herodian fortress on the hills east of the Dead Sea. Josephus gives a political reason (Antipas feared that John's influence could lead to an uprising), and the two accounts can stand side by side. John's question reflects the variety of expectations in Second Temple Judaism, the period from the rebuilding of the temple after the exile to its destruction in AD 70. Many Jews hoped for a Messiah, though they pictured him differently: a royal son of David, a priestly figure, a prophet like Moses, or the returning Elijah of Malachi 4:5.

Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, a short walk from Capernaum. Chorazin's basalt ruins, including a later synagogue, still stand in the hills above the lake. Tyre and Sidon were wealthy Phoenician ports on the Mediterranean coast, denounced by Old Testament prophets for their pride (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26 to 28), and Sodom was the byword for wickedness since Genesis 19. The parallel to Jesus' woes is Luke 10:13-15, and to his prayer, Luke 10:21-22.
cultural:
The picture of children in the marketplaces draws on everyday life. Children played at weddings, with flutes and dancing, and at funerals, with dirges and mourning. Jesus compares his generation to children who complain that the others won't play either game. John's austere life looked like madness; Jesus' feasting looked like indulgence. The critics were determined to reject both. Sackcloth, a coarse cloth usually made of goat hair, and ashes were the ordinary signs of mourning and repentance in the ancient Near East.

A yoke was a wooden frame laid across the necks of working animals so they could pull together. By Jesus' time Jewish teachers used it as an image for accepting the discipline of God's law; the Mishnah later speaks of taking on the yoke of the Torah. The Wisdom of Ben Sira (also called Sirach), a Jewish book from around 180 BC, has personified Wisdom invite the unlearned to come to her school and put their necks under her yoke, where they will find rest. Jesus' invitation takes up that language but speaks as Wisdom herself, not as one of her students.
literary: The chapter has three movements. Verses 1 to 19 concern John: his question, Jesus' answer drawn from Isaiah's promises, and Jesus' testimony to him. Verses 20 to 24 pronounce woes on unrepentant towns, set out in two parallel pairs with the same structure. Verses 25 to 30 turn from rebuke to prayer and invitation. The chapter's theme is recognition: John, the crowds, and the towns all fail to see clearly, while little children are given sight. Wisdom provides a quiet thread: wisdom is vindicated by her actions (verse 19), the wise and learned miss what children receive (verse 25), and Jesus speaks the invitation of Wisdom (verses 28 to 30). Verse 19 speaks of wisdom's actions where Luke 7:35 speaks of her children, and Matthew's wording links wisdom's actions with the works of Christ in verse 2.

outline.t: John's question from prison and Jesus' answer
A generation that would not listen
The Father reveals the Son to little children
Come to Me: the easy yoke

doctrines.note: Knowledge of God is given, not achieved. No one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him, and the Father has hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children. Humility, not learning, is the condition for receiving it.

Verse 27 describes a unique, mutual knowledge between the Father and the Son, and says all things have been entrusted to the Son. The church drew on passages like this for its confession of the Son's full deity and his eternal relation to the Father.

The woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum show that seeing God's works increases responsibility. Pagan cities would have repented at what these towns saw and ignored, so judgment is measured by the light a people received.

words.note: Zugos, yoke. The word pictures submission and work, and in Jewish teaching it stood for taking on God's law. Jesus does not offer freedom from every yoke; he offers his own, and calls it easy (chrestos, kind or well-fitting) because the one who lays it on is gentle and humble in heart.

Anapauo, to give rest or refresh. The noun form appears in verse 29, echoing Jeremiah 6:16, where God tells his people to walk in the good way and find rest for their souls. The rest Jesus offers is not idleness but relief from a burden carried alone.

Skandalizo, to cause to stumble or to take offense. A skandalon was the trigger of a trap or a stone to trip over. Jesus blesses the one who does not stumble over him, a gentle warning to John and to everyone whose picture of the Messiah does not match the Messiah who came.

Biazo, to use force. In verse 12 the verb can be read as passive (the kingdom suffers violence) or middle (the kingdom advances forcefully), and the related noun biastes describes violent or forceful people. The ambiguity makes this one of the hardest verses in the Gospels, discussed below.

christ: Jesus answers John not with a title but with a list of works that echo Isaiah 35:5-6 and 61:1, where the prophet describes the blind seeing, the lame leaping, the deaf hearing, and good news brought to the poor in the day of God's saving visit. By pointing to those works, Jesus identifies his ministry as the arrival of that day. He identifies John as the messenger of Malachi 3:1 who prepares the way, which makes Jesus the one for whom the way is prepared, the Lord who comes to his temple. In verse 27 he claims a knowledge of the Father that belongs to him alone, and in verses 28 to 30 he speaks as God's Wisdom and offers the rest that Israel's God promised. The one who makes these claims describes himself as gentle and humble in heart, the character he will show on the road to the cross.

hard.q: What does verse 12 mean when it says the kingdom has been subject to violence and the violent lay claim to it?
hard.a: The Greek verb in verse 12 can be read two ways, and the noun for violent people can be negative or neutral, so interpreters have offered several readings. The first, followed by the BSB, is that the kingdom suffers violence: since John began preaching, opponents have attacked it, as Herod imprisoned John and as the religious leaders oppose Jesus, and violent people try to seize or destroy it. The second reads the verb as the kingdom forcefully advancing, with the violent being either zealous revolutionaries trying to bring it in by force or, more positively, eager people pressing into it with determination (Luke 16:16 says everyone is forcing their way into it). A third combination holds that the kingdom is breaking in powerfully and also meeting violent resistance. The surrounding verses, which speak of John in prison and a generation that rejects God's messengers, lend some support to the first reading, but the question remains open among careful scholars. All readings agree that John's ministry marks a turning point: the time of the Law and the Prophets as promise has given way to the time of fulfillment.

questions: John, of all people, asked whether Jesus was the one. What does his question tell you about doubt in the life of a faithful person?
Jesus says the towns that saw the most were judged most strictly. What have you seen of God that makes you responsible to respond?
Jesus invites the weary and burdened to take his yoke. What burden are you carrying alone, and what might it mean to carry it yoked with him?
